cards.front: Recall a key point about Interest Rates, Saving and Borrowing
cards.back: An interest rate is the cost of borrowing or the reward for saving, expressed as a percentage of the amount.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Interest Rates, Saving and Borrowing
cards.back: Higher interest rates: encourage saving (better returns), discourage borrowing (more expensive loans), reduce spending (mortgages cost more, less disposable income), and reduce business investment (borrowing costs rise).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Interest Rates, Saving and Borrowing
cards.back: Lower interest rates: discourage saving, encourage borrowing and spending, stimulate investment, and can lead to inflation if demand grows too fast.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Interest Rates, Saving and Borrowing
cards.back: The Bank of England sets the base interest rate to control inflation — raising rates to cool the economy, lowering to stimulate it.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Interest Rates, Saving and Borrowing
cards.back: Factors influencing different interest rates: base rate, risk of borrower (higher risk = higher rate), length of loan, and competition between lenders.

cards.front: What should you know about economics exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating interest rate changes, use the SBI framework: Savers (how are they affected?), Borrowers (how are they affected?), Investment (what happens to business investment?). Interest rate changes have opposing effects on different groups.
Benefit: higher returns on deposits (e.g. Lose: lower returns on savings)
Lose: higher mortgage/loan repayments (e.g. Benefit: lower repayments)
Lose: more expensive to take new loans (e.g. Benefit: cheaper to borrow)
Mixed: higher borrowing costs but stronger pound (e.g. Mixed: cheaper borrowing but weaker pound)
Tend to fall as mortgages become costlier (e.g. Tend to rise as mortgages become cheaper)
Pound tends to strengthen (e.g. Pound tends to weaken)

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Higher interest rates are always bad for the economy. Correct: Higher rates are harmful for borrowers (higher mortgage costs, less disposable income, reduced business investment) but beneficial for savers (better returns on deposits, pension funds perform better).
